k729: Qerret asks €1,100–1,500/m² behind the villas and €2,200–2,500 on the first line, up 21–43% year on year.
k732: Rana e Hedhur is the dune belt north of Shëngjin and prices inside Shëngjin’s own €1,100–2,000/m² range, with the Dukagjini Residences premium running far above it — penthouses have listed up to €1.6m. The €70–80m Dukagjini Resort with a Swissôtel and a mini-marina is due in 2028. Now the part that matters more than any of that: this zone carries the single largest legal risk in the northern research. The dunes are a protected natural monument, and criminal proceedings over illegal construction and improper legalisation there name nine defendants including former heads of the Lezhë cadastre, with measures tightened on appeal in December 2025. Title and building-permit verification here is not diligence, it is the transaction.

k739: Rrashbull is inland Durrës, grouped with Shkozet in every source that covers it, and it exists for the buyer who wants the city without paying for sand. Expect roughly €1,000–1,500/m². That range is a reconciliation rather than a quote: Investropa puts the zone at €1,100–1,600 and Dyqani at €800–1,200, and the research settles between them. With no sea and no season, there is no summer spike in rents and no winter collapse either — it behaves like a normal residential market, which on this coast is unusual enough to be the point.

k746: Sarandë's centre asks €1,600–1,800/m² for turnkey stock, up from about €1,200/m² in 2022–23. The number worth sitting with is a different one: foreign demand has fallen two years running — down 50% in 2024 and another 30% in 2025 — while prices kept climbing. Rising prices on falling demand is a supply-side story, and it is the single most important thing to understand before buying in this city. The centre itself remains the practical choice for year-round use: walkable, serviced out of season, and a clear step below the promenade in price.

k751: Buzë Shëtitores is Sarandë's first line, along the promenade, at €3,000–3,500/m². Resort-branded apartments on it reach €4,000/m², and the coast tops out near €4,500 elsewhere. This is the most expensive stock the city sells, and it is priced on the view and the address rather than on what it earns: short-term rental in Sarandë runs at about 41% occupancy, which does not support these numbers on income alone. Buy here for use and for the asset, and treat any rental projection you are shown as the seller's arithmetic until you have checked it yourself.

k758: Shëngjin's seaside centre is, in practice, the whole Shëngjin market — the town has no second district that trades separately. It asks €1,100–2,000/m², with the mass segment at €1,100–1,500 and the top of the band going to premium residences on the front. Buyers are mostly Kosovar and from the diaspora, and a flat takes about three to three and a half months to sell. The state reference price is 49,200 lek/m², which is what notary and tax costs are calculated from rather than the price you agree.

k762: Shkëmbi has the widest gap between new and old stock in Durrës. New builds ask €1,200–2,000/m² while older apartments trade from €450 to €800/m², and the zone median lands at about €1,110/m². It sits roughly 150 m from the promenade, quiet and green by Durrës standards. That spread is the whole story of the zone: two markets under one name, and the cheap half is cheap for building age and condition, not for location. Check the construction year, the structure and the legal file before you read a low price per square metre as a bargain.

k767: Qendra is the historic core of Shkodra and its most expensive quarter. In a sample of listed asking prices gathered in August 2026, new builds ran at a median €1,457/m² and resale at €1,132/m², giving €1,377/m² across all 24 listings; the €1,700–1,900/m² quoted in agency surveys describes prime new stock only, not the quarter as a whole. At roughly 29% the new-build premium is the narrowest of the three researched quarters, because central resale stock holds its price. Buyers are mostly local families and northern diaspora rather than foreign investors, and Shkodra carries no short-term-rental economy of the kind that supports coastal prices, so the case for the centre rests on scarce building permits and on resale liquidity. All figures are asking prices, not transactions.

k773: Shkozë sits on what used to be the edge of Tirana and is now a line of new complexes along the Grand Ring, asking about €1,400/m². The road is the reason to look here and the reason to be careful: access is good and getting better, but shops, schools and everything else are still arriving. Its official reference rate, 97,200–102,800 lek/m², is the same band as Ali Demi, which puts the market price roughly a third above the state figure — a gap that has been closing across the city rather than widening.

k780: Shkozet is inland Durrës — a residential district on the main approach to the city, with no beach premium in the price. Sources disagree on what it costs: one puts it at €1,100–1,600/m², a local one at €800–1,200, and the honest answer sits between them. That disagreement is itself the useful signal. The zone is bought by local buyers and priced deal by deal rather than off a published rate, so comparable completed sales matter more here than any printed band. Road connectivity is the district's main argument.

k786:
Spille is the beach at the southern end of the Durrës coast, about 35 km from the city and administratively part of Rrogozhinë. The sand runs for kilometres with a pine belt behind it, and the lagoons near the mouth of the Shkumbin keep the area low-rise: a few small hotels on the front, holiday houses in the pines, and farmland in Rreth-Greth and Vilë-Bashtovë that is being sold as plots.

What is on the market here is mostly land, priced per square metre, plus hotel buildings and the first apartment blocks. It suits a buyer who wants a plot near the sea at a fraction of Golem prices and is prepared to wait for infrastructure; the road from Rrogozhinë is the only access and services are seasonal.

k792: Tale has the widest price spread on the northern coast. Raw stock 150 metres from the sea starts near €600/m², while the Talea Coast development asks €1,450–1,690 for the same distance to the same water. Nothing about the location explains a difference that large; the build quality, the developer and the paperwork do. Administratively this is Bashkia Lezhë, the same municipality as Shëngjin, and the research groups the two. One open question the knowledge base has not closed: the legal status of the land under the newer complexes. Ask for it in writing before you take the cheap end of that range seriously.

k799: Uji i Ftohtë is the coast immediately south of Vlora's promenade, priced at roughly €1,875–2,800/m². That band deserves a caveat the others do not: it is derived, not measured. The only source covering the zone states that it runs 20–25% below Lungomare, and the figures above apply that discount to the Lungomare range. Use them to size a budget, not to value a specific apartment, and ask the agent for comparable completed sales in the building before you make an offer.

k806: Velipoja is Shkodra’s beach, and the 2025 road cut the drive from Shëngjin from 66 km to under 15, which is the single biggest change to this market in a decade. Apartments ask €900–1,600/m². One oddity worth flagging: the state reference here is 60,400 lek/m² against Shëngjin’s 49,200, so the official map rates Velipoja higher than a market that actually trades dearer — the research marks this as illogical and unverified rather than explaining it away. The €280m Blue Borgo project is suspended amid title disputes with Rrjoll residents and a strategic-investor status the agency says is not active, so do not buy on the strength of it.
